lede: Darnell drafted a superteam and then took it apart with his own hands. Five players took $160 of his $200 — Jaylen Brown, Jalen Williams, Jalen Brunson, Paolo Banchero, Josh Hart — and every one of them was off the roster by day 99. Josh Hart lasted a single day. Jalen Williams never appeared in a lineup at all. What replaced them was better. Across thirteen trades and sixty-five waiver claims he rebuilt the entire roster by hand, took the third seed at 13–6, and finished seventh. This is a report about a team that was well managed and badly shaped.
profile: This is a punt build, executed with more conviction than anyone else in the league. Four categories he won at will; five he conceded before the season started. The volume table below shows what that costs. He led the league in field goals made and attempted, led it in threes, and finished 13th of 14 in field-goal percentage. That is not cold shooting across nineteen weeks — it is a roster of guards taking a lot of shots, which is exactly what wins PTS, 3PM and AST and exactly what loses FG%, REB and BLK.
ledger: Read it in two blocks. The left-hand columns — FG%, FT% — are almost solid red. The middle block is almost solid green. A team shaped like this has no margin. Nine of his twenty-one matchups came down to a single category, and he went 5–4 in them. Over a long regular season that is enough to finish third. In a one-week playoff round it is a coin flip, and in week 20 the coin came down on Optimize the MVPs by one category.
draft: $160 on the top five, and not one of them was still on the roster in March. Jaylen Brown at $34 started five games here and produced 2,874 for the season elsewhere. Brunson at $33 started eight and produced 2,762. Josh Hart at $27 was traded on day one. The bottom of the board is where the season actually came from. Jabari Smith Jr. at $4 returned 424 per dollar — second-best in the league behind Fantastic 5's Keyonte George at $3 — and Payton Pritchard at $12 returned 105. Two picks costing $16 between them outproduced the $160 above. Whether the expensive picks were mistakes depends on what came back for them, which is three sections down.
production: 72% of what this team scored came from players it did not draft. Through The Wire's figure was 44%, and most of the league sits nearer half. That is a remarkable amount of in-season roster construction, and the top of it worked: Brandon Ingram and Collin Gillespie were both acquired, and both outproduced every player he drafted. Ingram arrived on day 27 and started 129 of his 134 days on the roster — the most reliable thing about this team all year.
trades: Thirteen trades recovered from roster movement, against the fifteen ESPN counts. Ten of them can be graded on both sides, and those ten come out +1,900 in net production. He won his trades. The best is day 26: Quentin Grimes out, Brandon Ingram and Shaedon Sharpe in, +1,813 on its own and effectively the rest of the season's offence. The worst is day 43 — Jalen Duren and Ajay Mitchell for Donte DiVincenzo alone, −974, giving up two rotation players for one. The one that will annoy him is Jaylen Brown: acquired on day 18 for Brunson, gone again on day 30 after eleven starts, and worth 2,323 of production to somebody else afterwards.
wire: Sixty-five swaps at 0.42 net production per day is eighth of fourteen — mid-table, and behind Brockley Heat, who made ten moves all season and averaged 3.31. The churn kept the roster busy; it was not where the value came from.
bench: Mostly clean, with one that cost him. Jock Landale put up a 39 on the bench on day 95 — inside week 14, a matchup lost 4–5. One category, one benched centre, in the only category block where he had nothing to spare. Nineteen wasted player-days across a full season is otherwise ordinary. Lineup discipline was not this team's problem.
last: And here is the problem, stated as plainly as the data can state it. He set all ten starting slots on every single day of the matchup — 70 for 70. Nobody else in the league managed that. Those 70 starts produced 39 games: ten names a day, five and a half of whom played. The Infirmary set 51 slots, got 46 games, and won all nine categories. That is the bill for thirteen trades and sixty-five claims. The roster was full, and it was full of seventh men, two-way guards and rotation bigs whose NBA teams sat them. A deep roster of shallow players fills a lineup card and does not fill a box score.
closing:
The uncomfortable reading of this season is that Darnell was one of the best in-season managers in the league and it did not decide anything. He set his lineup every day, worked the wire harder than almost anyone, came out +1,900 on his trades, and carried a 13–6 record into the playoffs.

What beat him was shape, and shape was settled in the first month. A four-category team wins a long regular season on volume and then meets a single week where variance gets a vote. With no rebounding and no blocks to fall back on, a cold week from the guards left nothing underneath.

Two things would change it. Hold the categories he punted to a floor rather than zero — 33% in blocks and 43% in rebounds is not a punt, it is a leak, and one real big held all year closes it. And stop converting roster quality into roster quantity in March: by the last week he could fill every slot and only half of them played.
